content:
You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

If someone quits their job or is fired, what steps must they take to apply for Employment Insurance (EI) benefits, and how does Service Canada assess whether they qualify? Discuss what constitutes 'just cause' for quitting, how Service Canada determines misconduct for fired employees, and any recourse individuals have if Service Canada disqualifies their El claim. Include specific details from the application process, such as the importance of the Record of Employment (ROE) and the timeline for applying. Provide your response in 5-7 sentences.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Do I need my Record of Employment?
     2	 It is easier to apply for EI if you have your Record of
     3	 Employment (ROE). You will need an ROE for every employer
     4	 you worked for in the past 12 months.
     5	 If your employer sends your ROE to the government online:
     6	 ● they do not have to give you a copy, and
     7	 ● you do not need a copy to apply for EI.
     8	 But you can get a copy from Service Canada if you want one.
     9	 You need a My Service Canada account to see your ROE online.
    10	 Access your account or set one up at servicecanada.ca.
    11	 It is easier to apply for EI with your ROE. But you should apply
    12	 for EI right away, even if you do not have your ROE yet. You
    13	 will need proof of your employment, such as pay stubs and
    14	 T4 slips.
    15	 Employment Insurance | 5
    16	 If you do not apply within 4 weeks after your employment
    17	 ends, you will probably get fewer EI payments.
    18	 If you are having problems getting your ROE, call the
    19	 Employment Insurance Telephone Information Service at
    20	 1-800-206-7218. For TTY, call 1-800-529-3742.
    21	 CLEO has a tool that creates a letter you can send to your
    22	 employer asking for your ROE. Go to stepstojustice.ca/
    23	 asking-for-roe.
    24	 ❚❚❚ Can I get EI if I quit my job?
    25	 If you quit your job, you will not qualify for regular EI benefits
    26	 unless you had “just cause”. This means that you had to quit
    27	 because you had no other reasonable choice.
    28	 If you do not return to work when you are called back after a
    29	 layoff, Service Canada sees this as quitting your job.
    30	 If you have a problem at work, it helps to show that you tried
    31	 to fix it. If the problem is so serious that it cannot be fixed, you
    32	 might qualify for EI if you quit.
    33	 But you might want to start looking for another job before you
    34	 quit. Keep a record of your job search.
    35	 What if I had just cause for quitting?
    36	 If you can prove that you had just cause for quitting your job,
    37	 you can get EI. There are many situations that could be just
    38	 cause for quitting. Here are some examples.
    39	 6 | cleo.on.ca
    40	 You were discriminated against for one of the following
    41	 reasons:
    42	 ● your race, colour, national or ethnic origin, or religion
    43	 ● your sexual orientation or your sex, which includes
    44	 discrimination because of pregnancy or childbirth
    45	 ● your marital status or family status
    46	 ● your disability or age
    47	 ● you were convicted of a crime but have a pardon or
    48	 record suspension
    49	 ● you belong to a union
    50	 Your employer or supervisor:
    51	 ● refused to pay you for overtime work, or forced you to
    52	 work too much overtime
    53	 ● was unfair or hostile to you for no good reason
    54	 ● was doing something that was against the law
    55	 ● pressured you to leave your job
    56	 Or you quit your job because your employer:
    57	 ● expected you to work in dangerous conditions
    58	 ● cut your wages significantly or made major changes to
    59	 your duties
    60	 Even if one of the examples applies to you, that might not be
    61	 enough to be just cause. And there could be other reasons for
    62	 leaving that Service Canada will see as just cause.
    63	 It is best to get legal advice before you quit your job for any
    64	 reason. See page 27 to find out where to get legal help.
    65	 Employment Insurance | 7
    66	 ❚❚❚ Can I get EI if I was fired?
    67	 It depends on why you were fired. If Service Canada says
    68	 you were fired because of “misconduct”, they will not give
    69	 you benefits.
    70	 Misconduct usually means doing something wrong on
    71	 purpose. Misconduct is more than not being able to do the
    72	 job well. Here are some examples that could be misconduct:
    73	 ● threatening someone or being violent
    74	 ● destroying company property on purpose
    75	 ● being away from work without permission
    76	 ● not obeying an order from your employer
    77	 It is often unclear if what a worker does is misconduct.
    78	 Service Canada decides if you were fired for misconduct, not
    79	 your employer. So you should apply, even if you were fired.
    80	 ❚❚❚ If I quit or was fired, what happens when I
    81	 apply for EI?
    82	 When you apply, you have to answer questions on a special
    83	 form if you quit or were fired.
    84	 If you quit, you have to say:
    85	 ● why you quit
    86	 ● if you tried to fix the problem at work before you left
    87	 ● if you tried to get other work before you quit
    88	 8 | cleo.on.ca
    89	 If you were fired, you have to say:
    90	 ● why you were fired
    91	 ● if your employer gave you any warnings
    92	 ● if you tried to fix the problem
    93	 Once you have filled in the form, Service Canada may
    94	 interview you. They may also contact your employer. Then
    95	 they decide if you quit without having just cause or were fired
    96	 for misconduct.
    97	 Being disqualified
    98	 Service Canada could decide that you:
    99	 ● quit without having just cause, or
   100	 ● were fired for misconduct.
   101	 If this happens, they will tell you in a letter that you cannot get
   102	 regular EI benefits. This is called being “disqualified”.
   103	 The letter will also tell you that you have the right to ask them
   104	 to reconsider their decision. This means asking them to review
   105	 and change their decision.
   106	 You must ask for this in writing within 30 days of finding out
   107	 about Service Canada’s decision. For more information, see
   108	 page 25.
   109	 Even if you cannot get regular EI benefits, you might still be
   110	 able to get the special benefits that are listed

To apply, you need a Record of Employment (ROE) for every employer you worked for in the past 12 months, though "It is easier to apply for EI if you have your Record of Employment (ROE)" and "you should apply for EI right away, even if you do not have your ROE yet," using proof of employment such as pay stubs and T4 slips, because "If you do not apply within 4 weeks after your employment ends, you will probably get fewer EI payments" (doc.txt). When you apply, you must answer questions on a special form about why you quit or were fired, whether you tried to fix the problem, and whether your employer gave you warnings, after which "Service Canada may interview you. They may also contact your employer" (doc.txt). If you quit, you will not qualify for regular EI benefits "unless you had 'just cause'. This means that you had to quit because you had no other reasonable choice," with examples including discrimination, an employer refusing to pay overtime, dangerous working conditions, or significant wage cuts (doc.txt). If you were fired, benefits are denied only if Service Canada finds "misconduct," which "usually means doing something wrong on purpose," such as threatening someone, destroying company property on purpose, being away from work without permission, or not obeying an order, and "Service Canada decides if you were fired for misconduct, not your employer" (doc.txt). If Service Canada disqualifies you, they will tell you in a letter that you cannot get regular EI benefits, and "you have the right to ask them to reconsider their decision," which "must [be done] in writing within 30 days of finding out about Service Canada's decision" (doc.txt).
